candidate_claim_transitions.statement_amended: AMENDED, narrowed to what is left after the third repair. Three of the four items are closed in codes/loop/loop.sbatch and one is documented as intended. CLOSED (a): a SIGTERM seen during the pre-flight now stops the wrapper before the loop is launched -- SCHED_TERM is tested immediately above the launch, the wrapper says so, exits 143 and finalize books a scheduler termination with the count untouched and the successor kept (probe (i)-b: BEFORE the stand-in printed 'LOOP RAN AFTER THE SIGNAL' and the link exited 0; AFTER 'SIGTERM already received during the pre-flight -- not starting the loop', wrapper exit 143). CLOSED (b, the after-the-fact half): the loop's own status is recorded into LOOP_RC the instant it is known, on_term records whether that recording had already happened, and finalize lets a non-zero recorded status outrank a SIGTERM that arrived after it (probe (iii)-c: BEFORE 'scheduler termination ... failcount left at 0'; AFTER 'the loop had already exited rc=1 when the SIGTERM arrived -- counting the failure, not the signal', failcount 1). A recorded 143 past the runtime floor is deliberately NOT caught by that rule and stays a scheduler kill, so K1-K6 are unchanged. CLOSED (c): the loop writes $BASEDIR/.cycles_completed after every cycle whose five stages returned 0, the wrapper reads it at entry and in finalize, and a link that advanced it clears the failure run in both the scheduler-termination branch and the failure branch. KTG_MAX_FAILS=3 therefore means three failures with no completed cycle between them, which is what the header always claimed. Scenario O re-run with a cycle-recording loop gives 1,0,0,1,0,1 and does not trip; re-run with a loop that records nothing it still gives 1,1,1,2,2,3 and trips, as before. DOCUMENTED, not changed (d): KTG_MIN_RUNTIME_SECONDS, KTG_MAX_FAILS and KTG_MAX_CHAIN read the job environment and Slurm's default --export=ALL carries them down the whole chain; that is how an operator retunes a running chain without editing a file under a live job, so they stay knobs and the operating rule -- submit the first link from a clean shell -- is written next to them. KTG_RC_SIGTERM and KTG_RC_SCRATCH_STOP remain hard-coded. WHAT REMAINS OPEN, all reproduced in the same run: (r1) a loop status 143 arriving after KTG_MIN_RUNTIME_SECONDS is still read as a scheduler termination whatever caused it (probe (ii)-c) -- only Slurm job state can settle it, which is o25's; (r2) SCHED_TERM still outranks a deterministic pre-flight failure that happens after the signal, so probe (i)-c is booked as a scheduler termination and the successor self-corrects in one extra link (probe Ic2 counts it 1/3 and cancels its own successor); (r3) a signal landing in the two statements between the loop's return and the LOOP_RC/LOOP_RC_SET assignments is still read as a walltime end -- the window is irreducible without a lock and the direction is the safe one; (r4) the consequence of (c): a link that completes at least one cycle and then fails never accumulates, so a crash loop that manages a full cycle per link is bounded only by KTG_MAX_CHAIN=200 and not by the breaker (probe P5, count oscillating 2,2,2 over three links). Closes by an executed run under o25 that reads Slurm job state (TIMEOUT / CANCELLED / FAILED) back and confirms each classification, with the closing scenarios of o31 and this repair re-run.

candidate_result_row_amendment.claim: codes/loop/synchronous_loop_9x9.sh and codes/loop/export_model_for_selfplay_9x9.sh carry 'set -eu -o pipefail' in the body, so errexit, nounset and pipefail hold whether the file is executed or handed to `bash` -- the form loop.sbatch uses -- and a failure anywhere in the archive-staging section stops the loop instead of being followed by cycle 1 out of an incomplete archive. In codes/loop/loop.sbatch the .failcount accounting, the minimum-runtime penalty, the breaker and the scancel of the queued afterany successor live in one function, finalize(), run from an EXIT trap installed immediately after resubmit(), and finalize sorts the ways a link can end into five classes. A deliberate storage stop -- the loop exiting 3 WITH $BASEDIR/STOP present, the file the loop writes before that exit -- cancels the successor and spends no attempt. A scheduler termination -- SIGTERM to this wrapper, recorded by a TERM trap installed before the resubmit, or a 128+15 loop status on a link that has run at least KTG_MIN_RUNTIME_SECONDS -- keeps the queued successor, which is the resume itself, and leaves .failcount alone unless the link completed cycles, in which case the run of consecutive failures is cleared. A SIGTERM seen during the pre-flight ends the link before the loop is launched. A loop failure already recorded when a later SIGTERM arrives is counted as the failure it is. A pre-flight failure counts, with the fast-failure penalty, and cancels the successor. A loop failure counts and cancels only when the breaker trips; an exit 3 without STOP is one of these. A cycle that ran and exited 0 resets the count, an exit 0 that never ran the loop leaves it, and a link that advanced $BASEDIR/.cycles_completed restarts the failure run, so KTG_MAX_FAILS means three failures with no completed cycle between them. Neither loop.sbatch nor synchronous_loop_9x9.sh contains a storage threshold or its own du/df/quotas.py measurement: both call codes/data_budget/scratch_guard.sh and honour its exit code, with no --root passed. The three upstream defect repairs (o09, o13 config half, o17) admitted in the earlier rows are unchanged, and a KTG_STAGE_ONLY dry run from the real scratch clone stages the same 80 files byte-for-byte before and after this repair. NOT covered: a SIGKILL end -- KillWait expiry, cgroup OOM, node failure -- runs no handler, writes nothing and simply lets the queued successor resume, shown by scenario M; a loop status 143 after the runtime floor is still read as a scheduler termination whatever caused it; a SIGTERM already seen outranks a deterministic pre-flight failure that follows it, self-correcting in one extra link; and a link that completes a cycle before failing never accumulates toward the breaker. Nothing here ran on a GPU or under a real scheduler.
